## Solution

**Given:**
- Prevalence: P(disease) = 1/500 = 0.002
- Sensitivity: P(positive | disease) = 0.98
- Specificity: P(negative | no disease) = 0.95 → P(positive | no disease) = 0.05

**Apply Bayes' theorem:**

P(disease | positive) = [P(positive|disease) × P(disease)] / P(positive)

**Numerator:**
0.98 × 0.002 = 0.00196

**Denominator (total probability of testing positive):**
P(positive) = P(positive|disease)×P(disease) + P(positive|no disease)×P(no disease)
= (0.98 × 0.002) + (0.05 × 0.998)
= 0.00196 + 0.0499
= 0.05186

**Result:**
P(disease | positive) = 0.00196 / 0.05186 ≈ 0.037794...

Converting to a percentage: **3.78%**

This is the classic base-rate/screening paradox — even with a fairly accurate test, because the condition is rare (0.2% prevalence), most positive results are false positives. Out of every ~52 people who test positive, only about 2 actually have the condition.
